title: Cost, Monitoring and Reliability — Module Quiz

items.q: Which three numbers produce a daily cost estimate for a model-backed feature?
options: Model size, context length and number of users
Tokens per call, calls per day and price per token
Hosting cost, licence cost and support cost
items.explain: Input and output are usually priced separately, so estimate them separately too. Prices move, so take the current ones from the provider's own page.

items.q: A feature's limits are 200,000 tokens and 500 calls a day, and each call uses about 800 tokens. Which limit binds first?
options: The call limit, since 500 is the smaller number
The token limit, reached after about 250 calls
Neither, because the limits apply per month
items.explain: Two limits sit side by side and nothing says which matters. Dividing shows the token cap is reached long before the call cap.

items.q: Why must a budget be built on the worst case as well as the typical one?
options: Providers bill at the worst-case rate by default
It has to hold on the bad day, not the average one
Typical estimates are almost always too high
items.explain: A system that is affordable on average and ruinous on a busy day is not affordable.

items.q: Why is cost per unit of value more useful than a monthly total?
options: Monthly totals are routinely inaccurate
The same monthly figure can be good or bad depending on what it bought, and cost per unit shows how it scales
Providers do not publish monthly totals
items.explain: A hundred pounds that resolves three tickets is expensive; the same hundred resolving three thousand is not.

items.q: What are the only three ways to reduce the cost of a model-backed feature?
options: Cheaper hosting, fewer users and shorter answers
Fewer calls, less sent per call, and a smaller model
Caching, batching and prompt compression
items.explain: Every saving comes from one of the three. Caching and rules are ways of making fewer calls; trimming and compression send less; model choice is the third.

items.q: Why can cutting a system prompt purely for token cost be dangerous?
options: Shorter prompts always produce worse answers
Some sentences were added after something went wrong, so cutting by feel removes the protection
Providers charge more for short prompts
items.explain: Cut by testing. A sentence that looks like padding may be guarding against a failure that already happened once.

items.q: Why is an output ceiling set too low a false economy?
options: Output tokens are the cheapest to buy
A model that reasons spends the same allowance thinking, and with too little room the call can be billed and return nothing
Ceilings are ignored by most providers
items.explain: A ceiling that is too low does not save money. It risks a failure that costs and produces no answer.

items.q: Why is 'read the total, check it, make the call, add to the total' a race?
options: Reading and writing are slow operations
Many simultaneous requests can all read the old total and pass the check before any records its cost
Totals reset at midnight in the middle of requests
items.explain: The check and the record must be one step. A soft cap is right on a quiet day and wrong under load, which is when it is needed.

items.q: Why reserve the worst-case cost before a call and settle afterwards?
options: Settling is cheaper than reserving
A burst cannot collectively exceed the limit, and the reservation is corrected down to actual use afterwards
Providers require a reservation for every request
items.explain: Reserving an estimate afterwards is the original race. A failure to settle only over-counts the day, which is the safe direction to be wrong in.

items.q: A spending cap cannot read its own counter. What should it do?
options: Allow the call, because availability matters most
Refuse the call, because a cap that fails open works only when nothing is wrong
Allow it and log a warning for later
items.explain: It is the failures that produce surprise bills. For money, messages and record changes, fail closed.

items.q: A hard cap stops spending but sends no notification. What is missing?
options: A second, higher cap
An alert before the limit, so the owner finds out before the feature stops
A larger reservation per call
items.explain: A cap that stops the harm and leaves the owner to find out later is half a control. Alert at a fraction of the limit, somewhere a person reads.

items.q: Gemini reports reasoning tokens separately from the answer, and a cap counts only the answer. What follows?
options: The cap is slightly too strict
Recorded spend can be lower than the bill, so a cap enforced against the record undercounts
Nothing, because reasoning tokens are not charged
items.explain: A hard cap that undercounts is a soft cap with a confident label. Summing the two errs towards over-counting, which is the safe direction.

items.q: Why record the failure reason in the same row as the failure?
options: Rows with reasons take less storage
Otherwise diagnosis relies on someone relaying a log, and detail is lost at each copy
Providers require reasons to be stored for audit
items.explain: With the reason in the record, the answer is one query away. A diagnostic that depends on someone relaying it is not a diagnostic.

items.q: A single failure went unseen for five weeks. Which two gaps allowed it?
options: The count named nothing, and the window was shorter than the gap between looks
The failure was too small to log, and alerts were disabled
The provider hid the failure, and the console cached old data
items.explain: Group failures by reason so they are named, and keep the window much longer than the interval between looks.

items.q: What can a spend table not tell you?
options: How many tokens each call used
Whether the answers were good
Which model handled each call
items.explain: A system can be cheap, fast, reliable and wrong. Cost and quality are different measurements and need different records.

items.q: What does an HTTP 429 tell you?
options: That the provider is down
That you are over a limit, without saying which one or how long to wait
That your credentials were rejected
items.explain: Read the message and the pattern. A per-minute limit clears in a minute; a daily one does not clear until tomorrow.

items.q: How can you find a provider's real rate limit?
options: Read the pricing page for your tier
Count successes per minute across several runs; a stable number is the limit
Ask the provider's assistant
items.explain: The published figure may describe another tier or an older date. Measuring across repeated runs gives the number that actually binds.

items.q: How long should a retry wait after a per-minute rate limit?
options: About twenty seconds
Roughly a full minute, so the window actually ends
As short as possible, retrying repeatedly
items.explain: Twenty seconds cannot clear a per-minute limit. Retry once, not repeatedly, since a call that fails twice is telling you something.

items.q: Why make a long run against a tight limit resumable?
options: Resumable runs are cheaper to schedule
An interruption then costs only the gaps, not the whole run
Providers refuse runs that cannot resume
items.explain: A corpus finished over two sittings is not a worse result than one finished at once. Merge results and re-run only what did not complete.

items.q: A model appears in the provider's list but every call to it returns 404. What does the listing prove?
options: That the model works but your key is wrong
Only that the name is known, not that the model can still generate
That the provider is experiencing an outage
items.explain: Check by calling it, not by reading the catalogue. A label that says available when it only checked listed is a hazard.

items.q: Why condition a fallback retry on what you sent rather than on the provider's error message?
options: Error messages are never returned for rejected requests
An error string is someone else's wording and can change, while the request you sent is known with certainty
Provider messages are always too long to parse
items.explain: A fallback that waited for the message to mention the option never fired, because the real message named no field.

items.q: Why must a test set be run periodically and not only after your own changes?
options: Test sets expire after a set time
The provider changes things on its own timetable, with no change on your side
Platforms require periodic retesting for compliance
items.explain: Only a set run repeatedly and compared can tell real drift from the ordinary run-to-run variation that any single result contains.

items.q: Why can availability of a model differ between users of the same feature?
options: Providers rank users by account age
A request leaves from the location nearest the visitor, and the provider may not serve every region
Cached answers are served to some users
items.explain: A test from your own desk will not show it, and nothing in your configuration explains why one person succeeds and another does not.

items.q: A feature's spend counter cannot be reached. What should it do?
options: Fail open, since availability matters most
Fail closed, because money is at stake
Degrade to a cheaper model
items.explain: Choose per failure. Spending money, sending messages and changing records fail closed; an optional suggestion can fail open.

items.q: What makes the message 'search still works' safe to show during an outage?
options: It is short and reassuring
Search does not depend on the model, so the claim holds at the moment it is read
Learners will not try search anyway
items.explain: If the fallback described were checked right now, it should pass. A message promising more than the fallback delivers is worse than a plain error.

items.q: Why can a silent fallback model be a problem?
options: Fallback models always cost more
It can hide that the primary has been failing, and it gives answers you never tested
It makes timeouts longer
items.explain: A fallback behaves differently, needs its own testing and cost estimate, and if it takes over quietly nobody notices the primary failing.

items.q: What test decides whether a signal is worth watching?
options: Whether it is easy to collect
Whether someone will act on it
Whether competitors also track it
items.explain: A figure that never prompts a decision is clutter, and clutter buries the signal that matters.

items.q: What is the right way to write a runbook entry?
options: As a detailed essay on how the system works
As ordered steps for one symptom, calm to write and quick to follow by someone who did not build it
As a list of every error code the system can produce
items.explain: It is read in a hurry. Each step should exist because it once took a long time to find.
